HLD Cases: Core

System design, part 8 of 12

HLD Case Studies: Core

Eight worked high-level designs, the ones asked most often: URL shortener, rate limiter, key-value store, unique ID generator, notification system, news feed, chat and search autocomplete. Every case follows the same five steps, so you learn the rhythm as well as the answers. All numbers are order-of-magnitude assumptions chosen to make the arithmetic easy; in an interview, state yours and move on.

How to use these

Part 1 of 9 · the template and the map

Do not memorise the designs. Memorise the five steps and the two or three deep dives that make each problem different, then rebuild the rest from Building Blocks.

  • The five-step template: what to produce in each step and how long to spend
  • Building blocks per case: which earlier pages each case exercises

The five-step template

How to use these

Each case below has these five chapters, in this order. Timings assume a 45 minute interview.

StepWhat you produceTimeCommon mistake
1. Requirements and scale3 to 5 functional, non-functional with numbers, out of scope, a small estimate5 to 7 minEstimating everything; only compute numbers that change a decision
2. API and data model3 to 5 endpoints, main entities, the store and why5 minPicking a database before knowing the access pattern
3. High-level designOne diagram, read path and write path walked end to end10 minDrawing 25 boxes and explaining none
4. Deep dives2 to 4 hard parts, each with alternatives15 minWaiting to be asked; propose the deep dives yourself
5. Trade-offs and follow-upsDecisions with reasons, failure modes, what changes at 10x5 minPresenting the design as having no costs

Interview tip: the estimate exists to answer three questions: does it fit on one machine, is it read-heavy or write-heavy, and what is the hot path. Say the answer out loud after the arithmetic.

URL shortener

Part 2 of 9 · read-heavy key lookup

Map a long URL to a short key and redirect on lookup. It is asked because it is small enough to finish, yet forces a real decision on key generation, caching and the redirect status code.

  • Requirements and scale
  • API and data model
  • High-level design
  • Deep dives: key generation, the read path, aliases and expiry, analytics, scaling the store
  • Trade-offs and follow-ups

Requirements and scale

URL shortener

  • Functional: create a short URL for a long one; redirect short to long; optional custom alias; optional expiry; click counts per link.
  • Non-functional: redirect adds under about 50 ms at p99; redirects available 99.99%; a created link is never lost; keys are not trivially enumerable.
  • Out of scope: accounts and billing, malware and spam scanning, a dashboard UI.
QuantityArithmeticResult (approx.)
New URLsAssumption100 M per month
Write QPS100 M / (30 x 86,400 s = 2.6 M s)40 per second average, 200 peak (5x)
Read QPS100 reads per write: 10 B per month / 2.6 M s4,000 per second average, 12,000 peak (3x)
Daily users10 B / 30 = 333 M redirects per day, about 10 per user30 M DAU
Storage100 M x 12 x 5 years = 6 B rows x 500 bytes3 TB
Bandwidth4,000 per second x 500 bytes2 MB per second out
Key space62^73.5 x 10^12 keys, about 600x the 6 B needed
Cache20 M hot links x 500 bytes10 GB, one Redis node plus replica

What the numbers say: 100:1 read-heavy, 3 TB total, a 10 GB hot set. The whole problem is a cached key lookup; writes are almost irrelevant to capacity.

API and data model

URL shortener

  • Store: a key-value or wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) or sharded MySQL. Every query is a single-key get or a conditional put, with no joins, so pick for operational simplicity and replication.
  • Analytics: a columnar or time-series store fed from the event log, never the URL table.

High-level design

URL shortener

  • Write: Write API validates the URL, takes a key from the key service (or checks the custom alias), does a conditional insert, returns the short URL.
  • Read: Redirect service looks up the key in Redis; on a miss it reads the store, populates the cache with a TTL and answers with a redirect.
  • Analytics: the redirect emits a click event to a log without waiting for it; a stream job aggregates per key and day.
  • Stateless tiers: both services scale horizontally behind the load balancer; state is only in the store, cache and log.

Deep dives

URL shortener

Key generation

ApproachHowGainCost
Hash of the URLFirst 7 base62 characters of MD5 or SHA-256Stateless; same URL gives same keyCollisions need a check and retry with a salt; same-URL dedup is rarely wanted per user
Base62 of a counterEach server leases a range of ids, encodes the next oneUnique by construction, no read before writeSequential keys are enumerable; needs a range allocator
Pre-generated keysA key service creates random unused keys offline and hands out batchesUnguessable, no collision at write timeOne more stateful service; unused batches are lost on a crash (acceptable)
  • Collision odds for random keys: with 6 B keys used out of 3.5 x 10^12, a random key is taken about 0.17% of the time (6 x 10^9 / 3.5 x 10^12). Always insert with "put if absent" and retry.
  • Pick: counter ranges plus a permutation, or the key service. Both avoid a read before every write.

Read path: cache and 301 versus 302

StatusBrowser behaviourUse when
301 Moved PermanentlyCaches the mapping; later clicks may never reach youLowest load matters more than analytics, and targets never change
302 Found (or 307)Asks you every timeYou need click analytics, expiry, deletion or editable targets. The usual choice.

Custom aliases and expiry

  • Aliases share the key namespace: conditional insert, return 409 if taken. Reserve words (api, admin), restrict the alphabet, and keep generated keys at a fixed length that aliases may not use, so the two can never collide.
  • Expiry: check expires_at on read and answer 410; delete lazily with the store's TTL feature or a background sweep. Set the cache TTL to no more than the time left.
  • Do not recycle expired keys quickly: old links in the wild would point to a stranger's target.

Analytics as an async pipeline

  • The redirect never writes a counter synchronously. It appends an event (key, time, country, referrer) to a log such as Kafka and returns.
  • A stream job aggregates per key and minute or day with idempotent upserts, because delivery is at least once.
  • Trade-off: counts lag by seconds to minutes, and under overload you shed events, not redirects.

Scaling the store

  • Shard by hash of short_key; 3 TB over 5 years is a handful of shards, each replicated 3 times.
  • Most reads never reach it: with a 90% cache hit rate the store sees about 1,200 of the 12,000 peak reads per second.
  • Multi-region: replicate the store asynchronously and serve redirects from the nearest region; route creates to a home region or use region-prefixed key ranges to avoid conflicts.

Trade-offs and follow-ups

URL shortener

DecisionChoiceAlternativeWhy
Key generationCounter ranges plus permutationHash and retryNo read before write, no collisions
Redirect code302301Keeps analytics, expiry and edits working
StoreKV store, hash-shardedSingle relational primarySingle-key access, grows without resharding pain
Click countingAsync event logCounter update per redirectRedirect latency and availability do not depend on analytics
  • Failure mode: cache down. Redirects fall through to the store at 10x the usual load; keep replicas sized for it or shed with a small local in-process cache.
  • Failure mode: one viral link. It is a hot key, but a read-only one: a local cache in each redirect instance absorbs it.
  • Failure mode: range allocator down. Servers keep working from their leased range; lease early.
Follow-upOne-line answer
Same long URL submitted twice?Return a new key by default; dedup per owner needs an index on (owner, hash of URL).
How do you stop abuse?Rate limit creates per account and IP, check targets against a blocklist asynchronously, allow takedown by key.
How short can keys be?62^6 is 57 B, enough for the 6 B estimate; 7 leaves headroom and keeps random-key collisions rare.
Can users edit the target?Yes with 302: update the row and delete the cache entry.

Senior signal: you say early that this is a cached point lookup with a 10 GB hot set, spend the time on key generation and the 301 or 302 choice, and keep analytics off the redirect path without being asked.

Rate limiter

Part 3 of 9 · a check on every request

Decide, for each incoming request, whether a client is within its allowance. It is asked because the algorithm is easy and the distributed version is not: atomic counting, where the limiter sits, and what happens when its store fails.

  • Requirements and scale
  • API and data model
  • High-level design
  • Deep dives: algorithms, atomic counting in Redis, local versus global, placement, store failure, multi-region
  • Trade-offs and follow-ups

Requirements and scale

Rate limiter

  • Functional: limit requests per key (user, API key, IP) and per rule (endpoint, plan); several rules per request; reject with 429 and tell the client when to retry; change rules without a deploy.
  • Non-functional: adds about 1 ms at p99; limiter failure must not take the API down; accuracy within a few percent is acceptable; works across many gateway instances.
  • Out of scope: network-level DDoS protection, monthly billing quotas, bot detection.
QuantityArithmeticResult (approx.)
Active clientsAssumption50 M per day
Requests50 M x 170 per day = 8.5 B / 86,400 s100,000 per second average, 300,000 peak (3x)
Limiter checks2 rules per request x 300,000, sent as one script call300,000 Redis calls per second at peak
Storage50 M keys x 2 rules x 100 bytes10 GB of RAM
Bandwidth300,000 per second x 200 bytes per round trip60 MB per second inside the data centre

What the numbers say: memory is trivial; throughput is not. One Redis shard handles on the order of 100,000 simple operations per second, so plan several shards keyed by client, or avoid the network hop for most requests.

API and data model

Rate limiter

DataShapeStore and reason
Countersrl:{rule}:{key}:{window} to an integer with a TTL, or a hash {tokens, last_refill}Redis: in-memory, atomic increments and scripts, built-in expiry
RulesRule id, match, key, limit, window, algorithmRelational table or config repo; pushed to every limiter and cached in memory
DecisionsSampled allow and reject eventsMetrics and logs, for tuning limits and spotting abuse

High-level design

Rate limiter

  • Request path: the middleware matches the request to its rules, builds the keys, and runs one atomic script in Redis that updates the counters and returns the decision.
  • Allowed: forward to the backend and add the rate limit headers. Rejected: answer 429 with Retry-After; the backend never sees the request.
  • Rule path: operators change rules in the rules service; limiters receive them by push or poll and keep them in memory, so the hot path reads no database.
  • Sharding: Redis Cluster shards by key; put the client id in a hash tag so all counters for one client land on one shard and one script can touch them.

Deep dives

Rate limiter

Algorithms recap

The mechanics are in Building Blocks; this is the comparison to have ready.

AlgorithmState per keyBurstsWeaknessUse when
Token bucketTokens, last refill timeAllowed up to bucket sizeTwo parameters to tuneDefault for public APIs
Leaky bucketQueue or level, last leak timeSmoothed awayBursts wait or dropProtecting a backend that needs a steady rate
Fixed windowOne counterUp to 2x the limit across a boundaryBoundary spikeCoarse quotas (per day)
Sliding logA timestamp per requestExactMemory grows with the limitLow limits that must be exact
Sliding window counterTwo countersApproximately exactAssumes even spread in the previous windowHigh limits, cheap and accurate enough

Distributed counting with Redis

  • INCR then EXPIRE from the client is a second race: if the client dies between the two commands the key never expires and the client stays blocked for good. A Lua script (or SET key 0 EX 60 NX followed by INCR) closes it, because Redis runs a script as one unit.
  • Token bucket in Redis is the same idea: one script reads {tokens, last_refill}, refills by elapsed time, subtracts the cost and writes back.
  • Use Redis server time inside the script, or pass a time from one source; gateway clocks disagree.

Local versus global limits

ModeGainCost
Local only (limit / instances each)No network hop, no dependencyWrong when load is uneven or instance count changes
Global (Redis on every request)AccurateA hop per request, Redis on the critical path
Hybrid (leased batches)Redis load drops by the batch sizeOvershoot up to batch size x instances; more code

Placement

WhereGainCostUse for
API gateway or edgeOne place, rejects before any backend workKnows little about business cost of a callPer-client and per-IP limits on public APIs
Sidecar proxyLanguage independent, per-service rulesNeeds a mesh; an extra local hopService-to-service limits
Library in the serviceCan limit by business meaning (per tenant, per expensive query)One implementation per language, upgrades are slowFine-grained internal limits

When the limiter store is down

PolicyBehaviourChoose for
Fail openAllow traffic, alert, fall back to a coarse local limitMost APIs: a limiter outage should not become a product outage
Fail closedReject until the store is backLimits that are a security or cost control: login attempts, OTP sends, paid third-party calls

Give the Redis call a tight timeout (a few milliseconds) and a circuit breaker; a slow limiter is worse than a missing one.

Multi-region

  • Per-region limits: split the quota by region. Simple, no cross-region latency; a client that roams can get up to the sum.
  • Shared global limit: each region counts locally and replicates counts asynchronously. Approximate by the replication lag, which is usually acceptable.
  • Never make a synchronous cross-region call on the request path: it costs tens of milliseconds and couples regions.

Trade-offs and follow-ups

Rate limiter

DecisionChoiceAlternativeWhy
AlgorithmToken bucketSliding window counterAllows short bursts, two numbers of state
AtomicityLua scriptMULTI / EXEC, or client-side locksOne round trip, read and write in one unit
PlacementGatewayLibrary in each serviceCentral rules, rejects early
Store failureFail open with local fallbackFail closedAvailability of the API comes first
AccuracyApproximate (leases, async replication)Exact global countExactness costs a synchronous hop everywhere
  • Failure mode: hot key. One huge tenant puts all its counting on one shard; lease batches locally or split the tenant's key into sub-keys.
  • Failure mode: Redis failover loses recent counters (asynchronous replication). Clients get a brief extra allowance; accept it.
  • Failure mode: rejected clients retry at once and add load. Send Retry-After and make 429 responses cheap.
Follow-upOne-line answer
Different cost per endpoint?Pass a cost to the bucket: an expensive call takes several tokens.
Limit by IP behind NAT?IP is a weak identity; prefer API key or user, keep IP limits loose.
Hard versus soft limits?Soft limits log or throttle (queue, slow down); hard limits reject.
How are rules updated safely?Versioned config, staged rollout, and a shadow mode that counts without rejecting.

Senior signal: you name the race before the interviewer does, state the fail-open or fail-closed choice per rule and not globally, and offer shadow mode for rolling out a new limit.

Key-value store

Part 4 of 9 · Dynamo-style, always writable

Design a distributed store for get and put that survives node and network failures. It is asked because it tests the core of distributed data: partitioning, replication, consistency and repair. The design below follows the published Dynamo paper, which Cassandra and Riak also build on.

  • Requirements and scale
  • API and data model
  • High-level design
  • Deep dives: partitioning and quorums, versioning, failure handling and repair, storage engine, when to use consensus
  • Trade-offs and follow-ups

Requirements and scale

Key-value store

  • Functional: put(key, value), get(key), delete(key); opaque values up to about 1 MB; consistency tunable per request.
  • Non-functional: writes accepted even during node failure or partition (AP); p99 under about 10 ms; add nodes with no downtime; no single point of failure; each key on 3 replicas.
  • Out of scope: range scans, secondary indexes, multi-key transactions.
QuantityArithmeticResult (approx.)
CallersInfrastructure: clients are services, not end usersDAU not applicable
QPSAssumption: 200,000 reads + 50,000 writes per second250,000 per second average, 500,000 peak (2x)
Logical data10 B keys x 1 KB10 TB
Physical data10 TB x 3 replicas30 TB
Nodes30 TB / 2 TB per node = 15, kept about 60% fullAbout 25 nodes
BandwidthClient: 250,000 x 1 KB; replication: 50,000 x 1 KB x 3250 MB per second client, 150 MB per second between nodes

What the numbers say: a few dozen nodes, each serving about 20,000 operations per second at peak. Small enough that every node can know the whole ring, which is what makes one-hop routing and gossip practical.

API and data model

Key-value store

Stored per keyPurpose
Key, value (opaque bytes)The data; partition is chosen by hash of the key
Version (vector clock or timestamp)Decide which copy is newer, or detect that two are concurrent
Tombstone flag and timeA delete is a write, so it replicates and is not undone by a stale replica; purged after a grace period

Each node persists its share in a local LSM-tree engine (see the deep dive). There is no schema and no central metadata store; ring membership is the only shared state.

High-level design

Key-value store

  • Routing: the client (or a load balancer) reaches any node; that node hashes the key, finds the N replicas on the ring and acts as coordinator.
  • Write: coordinator sends the put to all N, returns success after W acks; the rest finish in the background.
  • Read: coordinator asks all N, returns after R replies, reconciles versions and repairs stale replicas.
  • Failure: if a replica is down, another node takes the write with a hint and hands it back later.
  • Symmetry: every node has the same role. No leader, so no failover; the price is conflict handling.

Deep dives

Key-value store

Partitioning and quorums

  • Consistent hashing with virtual nodes: each physical node owns many small ranges of the hash ring, so adding or losing a node moves about 1/n of the keys and spreads the load over many peers.
  • Preference list: the first N distinct physical nodes clockwise from the key, ideally in different racks or zones.
N, W, RPropertyUse when
3, 2, 2R + W > N: every read quorum overlaps the last write quorum; tolerates one node down for bothDefault
3, 1, 1Fastest; reads can be staleCaches, metrics
3, 3, 1Fast consistent reads; a write fails if any replica is downRead-heavy, rarely written
3, 1, 3Fast writes; a read fails if any replica is downWrite-heavy ingestion

Trade-off: R + W > N is not linearizability. Sloppy quorums, concurrent writers and partial write failures can still return stale or conflicting versions.

Versioning and conflict resolution

StrategyGainCost
Vector clocks, siblings returned to the clientNo silent data lossClient must merge; clocks grow and need pruning
Last write wins by timestampSimple, no siblings (the Cassandra default)Clock skew silently drops a write
CRDT values (counters, sets)Merge is automatic and correctOnly for data types with a defined merge

Failure handling and repair

ProblemMechanismHow it works
Replica briefly downSloppy quorum and hinted handoffThe next healthy node accepts the write with a hint naming the owner and replays it when the owner returns
Replica missed a writeRead repairOn a read the coordinator sees an old version and pushes the newest to that replica
Cold data diverged, or a node was replacedAnti-entropy with Merkle treesReplicas compare hash trees per key range and transfer only the ranges that differ
Who is in the cluster, who is deadGossipEach node exchanges membership and heartbeat state with a few random peers every second; state spreads in O(log n) rounds

Storage engine

  • LSM tree (RocksDB, Cassandra): sequential writes, good compression; pays with compaction I/O and reads that may touch several files. The usual choice here.
  • B-tree (InnoDB): predictable reads, in-place updates; random write I/O. Choose for read-heavy workloads with many range scans.

When to choose consensus instead

Dynamo-style (leaderless)Consensus-based (Raft or Paxos per shard)
ConsistencyEventual, tunableLinearizable
During a partitionBoth sides accept writesOnly the majority side
ConflictsPossible, must be resolvedNone
Compare-and-set, locks, unique constraintsNot safelyYes
ExamplesCassandra, Riak, the original Dynamoetcd, ZooKeeper (ZAB), CockroachDB, TiKV
Use forCarts, sessions, feeds, time seriesConfiguration, leader election, balances, inventory

Trade-offs and follow-ups

Key-value store

DecisionChoiceAlternativeWhy
ReplicationLeaderless quorumLeader per shard with consensusAlways writable, no failover step
PartitioningConsistent hashing with vnodesRange partitioningEven load, cheap rebalancing; gives up range scans
ConflictsVector clocksLast write winsNo silent loss; more work for clients
EngineLSM treeB-treeWrite throughput
  • Failure mode: a deleted key comes back. A replica that was down longer than the tombstone grace period still has the old value and repair copies it back. Repair every node within the grace period.
  • Failure mode: hints pile up during a long outage. Cap hint storage and rely on Merkle repair afterwards.
  • Failure mode: hot key. Hashing spreads keys, not load per key; cache in front or split the key in the application.
Follow-upOne-line answer
How does a new node join?It announces itself by gossip, takes over vnode ranges, and streams those ranges from the current owners before serving.
How do you detect a dead node?Missed gossip heartbeats, judged by a suspicion level and not one fixed timeout (the phi accrual detector in Cassandra).
Multi-datacentre?Place replicas per datacentre and use a local quorum for latency; replicate across asynchronously.
Read-your-writes?R + W > N with strict quorums gets close; for a hard guarantee use a consensus-based store.

Senior signal: you separate the four repair mechanisms by the failure each one covers, say plainly that quorum overlap is not linearizability, and can state when you would not build this and would use a consensus-based store instead.

Unique ID generator

Part 5 of 9 · coordination-free uniqueness

Produce unique, roughly time-ordered 64-bit ids at high rate from many machines. It is asked because the answer fits on a whiteboard and still probes clocks, coordination and failure handling.

  • Requirements and scale
  • API and data model
  • High-level design
  • Deep dives: the options, clock skew, worker ids, multiple datacentres
  • Trade-offs and follow-ups

Requirements and scale

Unique ID generator

  • Functional: ids are unique across all machines and datacentres; fit in a signed 64-bit integer; sort roughly by creation time; can be generated in batches.
  • Non-functional: 100,000 ids per second at peak; under 1 ms per id; no network call per id; keeps working when the coordination service is down.
  • Out of scope: gapless sequences (invoice numbers), unguessable ids (use random tokens for secrets).
QuantityArithmeticResult (approx.)
CallersInfrastructure: called by other servicesDAU not applicable
QPSAssumption10,000 per second average, 100,000 peak
Ids per day10,000 x 86,400864 M
StorageThe generator keeps no idsNone (8 bytes per id wherever it is used)
Bandwidth100,000 x 8 bytes0.8 MB per second, negligible
Capacity per worker2^12 = 4,096 per ms x 1,0004 M per second
Lifetime2^41 ms / (3.15 x 10^10 ms per year)69 years from the chosen epoch

What the numbers say: one worker covers the peak 40 times over. Workers are added for availability and locality, not throughput.

API and data model

Unique ID generator

The "data model" is the bit layout of the id (the Snowflake layout published by Twitter):

BitsFieldRangeNote
1SignAlways 0Keeps the id positive in signed languages
41Milliseconds since a custom epoch69 yearsHighest bits, so ids sort by time
10Worker id (5 datacentre + 5 machine)1,024 workersMust be unique among live workers
12Sequence within the millisecond4,096 per msResets to 0 each millisecond

High-level design

Unique ID generator

  • Startup: a worker leases a unique worker id from the coordination service and reads the last timestamp it used (if persisted).
  • Generate: read the clock, bump the sequence if the millisecond is unchanged, pack the three fields. No I/O.
  • Deployment: as a library inside each service (no hop, but every instance needs a worker id) or as a small service called in batches.
  • Ordering: ids from one worker are strictly increasing; across workers they are ordered to within clock sync error (k-sorted).

Deep dives

Unique ID generator

The options

OptionSizeOrderedCoordinationCost
UUID v4 (random)128 bitsNoNoneToo wide for the requirement; random inserts fragment B-tree indexes
UUID v7 (time + random)128 bitsYesNoneStill 128 bits; a good default when 64 bits is not required
DB auto-increment, stepped (server k of n issues k, k+n, ...)64 bitsPer server onlyA database write per idHard to add servers; the database is the bottleneck
Ticket server with ranges64 bitsRoughlyOne call per range of, say, 1,000 idsCentral service to keep available; ids reveal volume
Snowflake-style64 bitsBy time, k-sortedOnly at startupDepends on clocks; worker ids must be managed

Clock skew and going backwards

  • Why it goes backwards: NTP step corrections, VM migration, leap second handling. Configure NTP to slew, not step.
  • Restart hazard: a restarted worker forgets its last timestamp. Persist it periodically (and start from the persisted value plus a margin), or take a fresh worker id on every start.
  • Alternative: treat the timestamp field as a logical clock that only moves forward and may run slightly ahead of wall time under bursts.

Worker id assignment

MethodGainCost
Static configurationNo dependencyManual, breaks with autoscaling; a copy-paste error gives duplicate ids
Lease from etcd or ZooKeeperSafe with autoscaling; ids are reused after a lease expiresNeeded at startup; must stop generating if the lease is lost
Derive from IP or host nameNo coordinationCollisions unless the address space maps cleanly into 10 bits

Multiple datacentres

  • Reserve the top bits of the worker id for the datacentre; each datacentre then assigns machine bits on its own, with no cross-site calls.
  • Uniqueness holds globally. Ordering across sites is only as good as clock sync (typically milliseconds with NTP), so never use id order as proof of causality.

Trade-offs and follow-ups

Unique ID generator

DecisionChoiceAlternativeWhy
SchemeSnowflake-styleTicket server with rangesNo call per id or per range, time-sortable
Bit split41 / 10 / 12More worker bits, fewer sequence bitsTune to fleet size; 4,096 per ms per worker is rarely needed
Worker idsLeasedStaticSafe under autoscaling
Clock moving backWait or refuseKeep generatingDuplicates are worse than a brief outage of one worker
  • Failure mode: two workers with the same worker id produce duplicates silently. Fence with leases, and keep a unique constraint where the ids are stored.
  • Failure mode: coordination service down. Running workers continue; only new workers cannot start.
  • Failure mode: ids leak information (creation time, rough volume). Do not expose them where that matters.
Follow-upOne-line answer
Need strictly increasing ids globally?That needs a single sequencer or consensus; expect a throughput and availability cost.
JavaScript clients?Numbers above 2^53 lose precision; send ids as strings in JSON.
What after 69 years?Pick a recent custom epoch; widening the timestamp later means a new id format.
Why do sorted ids help the database?Inserts append to the right edge of the index, and the id doubles as a creation-time sort key.

Senior signal: you raise clock regression and duplicate worker ids yourself, and you size the bit fields from the numbers instead of reciting 41 / 10 / 12.

Notification system

Part 6 of 9 · reliable delivery through third parties

Send push, SMS and email on behalf of many internal services. It is asked because the delivery itself is outsourced, so the design is all about queues, retries, duplicates, limits and provider failure.

  • Requirements and scale
  • API and data model
  • High-level design
  • Deep dives: deduplication, retries and dead letters, priority and per-user limits, provider failover and tracking
  • Trade-offs and follow-ups

Requirements and scale

Notification system

  • Functional: send by push (APNs for iOS, FCM for Android), SMS and email; templates with parameters; per-user channel preferences and opt-out; delivery status per notification; scheduled and bulk sends.
  • Non-functional: transactional messages (OTP, payment alerts) leave within about 2 seconds; promotional within minutes; at-least-once with no user-visible duplicates; a slow provider must not block other channels.
  • Out of scope: building an SMTP or SMS gateway, an in-app inbox, the campaign authoring tool.
QuantityArithmeticResult (approx.)
UsersAssumption100 M DAU
Notifications100 M x 10 per day1 B per day: 800 M push, 150 M email, 50 M SMS
QPS1 B / 86,400 s11,600 per second average, 58,000 peak (5x, campaigns)
Storage1 B x 500 bytes of delivery log per day x 30 days kept500 GB per day, 15 TB retained
Bandwidth11,600 x 1 KB payload12 MB per second average, 58 MB per second peak

What the numbers say: the 5x bursts come from campaigns, and providers throttle you. Queues absorb the burst; the design question is how to stop a campaign from delaying an OTP.

API and data model

Notification system

  • Preferences, devices, templates: relational or KV store, read on every send, so cached.
  • Notifications and deliveries: append-heavy, queried by id or by user and time, expired after 30 days: a wide-column store with TTL.

High-level design

Notification system

  • Accept: the API authenticates the caller, deduplicates on the idempotency key, loads preferences, drops opted-out channels, and enqueues one message per remaining channel. It answers 202 once the messages are durably queued.
  • Send: a channel worker renders the template, applies per-user and per-provider rate limits, calls the provider and records the result in the delivery log.
  • Track: providers report delivered, bounced or failed through webhooks; a small consumer updates the delivery row.
  • Bulk: a campaign is expanded into per-user messages by a separate job that feeds the promotional queues at a controlled rate.

Deep dives

Notification system

Deduplication and idempotency

Where duplicates come fromDefence
Caller retries the API call after a timeoutIdempotency key: SET key NX with a 24 hour TTL, or a unique index; return the first notification id
Queue redelivers after a worker crash (at-least-once)Worker checks and conditionally updates the delivery row for (notification id, channel) before sending
Worker sent, then crashed before recording itCannot be fully closed; pass a stable message id or collapse key to the provider where it supports one (apns-collapse-id, FCM collapse_key)
Two services send the same eventDerive the idempotency key from the business event, not from the request

Trade-off: exactly-once delivery to a phone does not exist. Aim for at-least-once with deduplication, and decide per message type whether a rare duplicate or a rare loss is worse.

Retries, backoff and dead-letter queues

  • Backoff: exponential with jitter, for example 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, 16 s, then dead-letter. Honour the provider's Retry-After.
  • TTL per message type: an OTP that is 2 minutes late is noise; drop it instead of retrying.
  • Dead-letter queue: holds what could not be sent, with the reason, for alerting and replay after a fix. Alert on its growth rate.
  • Implement the delay with a delayed queue or a retry topic per backoff tier, not by sleeping in the worker.

Priority and per-user rate limits

  • Per user: a cap on promotional messages (say 3 per day per channel) and quiet hours in the user's time zone; transactional messages bypass both.
  • Per provider: a token bucket at the provider's agreed rate, with transactional traffic taking tokens first.

Provider failover and delivery tracking

  • SMS and email have interchangeable vendors, so keep two integrated and send a little traffic to the secondary all the time. Push has no substitute: APNs and FCM are the only route to their devices, so queue and retry.
  • Failover risk: a message accepted by A just before the breaker opened may be re-sent through B. This is the duplicate case above.
  • Tracking: "sent" means the provider accepted it; "delivered" needs a receipt, which push gives only partially. Opens and clicks come from the client or tracked links.

Trade-offs and follow-ups

Notification system

DecisionChoiceAlternativeWhy
CouplingQueue per channel and prioritySynchronous send from the APIIsolation, burst absorption, retries
GuaranteeAt-least-once plus dedupAt-most-onceA lost OTP is worse than a rare duplicate
Preferences checkAt accept time, re-checked at send for delayed messagesOnly at acceptOpt-outs must take effect for queued campaigns
ProvidersTwo per channel where possibleOneVendor outages are common
  • Failure mode: retry storm against a degraded provider. Backoff with jitter, a breaker and a provider rate limit.
  • Failure mode: a poison message crashes every worker that takes it. Cap attempts and dead-letter it.
  • Failure mode: a campaign targets the wrong segment. Throttled ramp-up and a kill switch that purges the campaign's queued messages.
Follow-upOne-line answer
Scheduled sends?Store with a due time; a scheduler scans due buckets and enqueues, idempotently.
User has five devices?Fan out to every valid token; use a collapse key so a newer message replaces an older one.
Order of notifications?Not guaranteed across channels; within a channel partition the queue by user if order matters.
How do you know it works?Per channel: accept-to-send latency, provider error rate, delivery rate, dead-letter rate.

Senior signal: you separate transactional from promotional traffic in the first diagram, classify errors as transient or permanent before talking about retries, and admit where a duplicate can still slip through.

News feed and timeline

Part 7 of 9 · fan-out and precomputed reads

Show each user recent posts from the accounts they follow. It is asked because of one decision with no free answer: do the work when a post is written, or when a feed is read, and what to do about accounts with millions of followers.

  • Requirements and scale
  • API and data model
  • High-level design
  • Deep dives: fan-out strategies, feed storage, ranking and cursors, media, counters, consistency
  • Trade-offs and follow-ups

Requirements and scale

News feed and timeline

  • Functional: publish a post (text plus media); follow and unfollow; load the home feed, newest or ranked, with paging; like a post and see like counts.
  • Non-functional: feed load under 200 ms at p99; a new post appears for followers within a few seconds (eventual consistency is fine); feed reads stay available when the write side is degraded.
  • Out of scope: ads, search, direct messages, recommending accounts the user does not follow.
QuantityArithmeticResult (approx.)
UsersAssumption200 M DAU
Feed reads200 M x 5 per day = 1 B / 86,400 s11,600 per second average, 35,000 peak (3x)
Posts200 M x 0.5 per day = 100 M / 86,400 s1,160 per second
Fan-out writes100 M posts x 200 followers average = 20 B per day230,000 timeline inserts per second
Post storage100 M x 1 KB per day x 365100 GB per day, 36 TB per year
Media storage20% of posts x 500 KB = 20 M x 0.5 MB10 TB per day, in object storage
Timeline cache200 M users x 500 entries x 16 bytes1.6 TB of RAM
Bandwidth11,600 x 20 posts x 1 KB230 MB per second of JSON; media goes through the CDN

What the numbers say: reads outnumber posts 10 to 1, but fan-out multiplies each post by 200, so the write side does 20 times more work than the read side. That ratio is the whole problem.

API and data model

News feed and timeline

DataStoreReason
PostsSharded KV or wide-column, keyed by a time-sortable post idPoint reads by id, huge volume, no joins
Follow graphSharded store with both directions, cachedTwo access patterns, long lists
TimelinesRedis sorted set of post ids per userPrecomputed feed, read in one call
MediaObject store behind a CDNLarge immutable blobs

High-level design

News feed and timeline

  • Post: the post service stores the post and emits an event; it answers the author without waiting for fan-out.
  • Fan-out: workers read the author's followers in pages and push the post id into each follower's timeline.
  • Read: the feed service takes a page of ids from the timeline cache, fetches the posts and authors (a multi-get, mostly from cache), drops deleted or blocked items, and returns them with a cursor.
  • Media: clients upload directly to the object store with a presigned URL and download through the CDN; the API tier never carries the bytes.

Deep dives

News feed and timeline

Fan-out on write, on read, or hybrid

StrategyWrite costRead costBreaks when
Fan-out on write (push)One insert per followerOne cache readAn account has millions of followers; work is wasted on inactive users
Fan-out on read (pull)One insertQuery every followee and mergeA user follows thousands; read latency grows
HybridPush for normal accounts, nothing for celebritiesCache read plus a merge of a few celebrity listsMore code paths; needs a threshold (say 100,000 followers)

The arithmetic that justifies hybrid: one post from an account with 100 M followers is 100 M cache writes. At 100,000 writes per second that is about 17 minutes of fan-out for a single post, delaying everything behind it.

Feed storage, ranking and cursors

  • Storage: one Redis sorted set per user, member and score both the time-sortable post id; trimmed to the newest 500 or so. Store ids only, never post bodies.
  • Inactive users: skip them in fan-out and rebuild the timeline by pull on their next visit. This removes a large share of the 230,000 inserts per second.
  • Ranking: a common design takes a few hundred candidates from the timeline and scores them with a model using features such as recency, affinity to the author and predicted engagement. Chronological order is the fallback when the ranker is slow or down.
  • Cursor, not offset: the cursor is the last post id seen (opaque to the client); the next page is "ids below the cursor". Offsets skip or repeat items because new posts shift every position.

Media through a CDN

  • Upload: presigned URL straight to the object store; an asynchronous job makes thumbnails and renditions; the post references media by id.
  • Download: immutable, versioned URLs with long cache lifetimes, so the CDN serves nearly all of the 10 TB per day.

Like counters

  • Truth is the POST_LIKE row (post, user): it makes a like idempotent and answers "did I like this".
  • The count is a denormalised counter updated asynchronously from like events, cached, and allowed to lag by seconds.
  • Hot posts: buffer increments in memory and flush in batches, so one viral post does not cause thousands of writes per second to one row.

Consistency expectations

WhoExpectationHow
AuthorSees own post at onceInsert into the author's own timeline synchronously, or merge it on the client
FollowersSee it within secondsAsynchronous fan-out; monitor fan-out lag
EveryoneDeleted posts disappearFilter at hydrate time; lazily remove ids from timelines
UnfollowNo new posts from that accountFilter at read; old entries age out

Trade-offs and follow-ups

News feed and timeline

DecisionChoiceAlternativeWhy
Fan-outHybridPure push or pure pullFast reads for most users without celebrity write storms
Timeline contentPost ids onlyFull postsSmall, and edits or deletes need no rewrite
PagingCursor on post idOffsetStable under inserts
CountersAsynchronous, approximateTransactional countWrite throughput on hot posts
  • Failure mode: timeline cache node lost. Timelines are derived data: rebuild by pull on demand, and replicate the cache to keep rebuild load small.
  • Failure mode: fan-out backlog. Feeds go stale but stay readable; scale workers, and prioritise active followers.
  • Failure mode: hydrate fan-in. One feed page needs 20 posts and authors; use multi-gets and a per-request deadline, and return a partial page over an error.
Follow-upOne-line answer
A user follows a new account?Merge that account's recent posts into the timeline asynchronously.
Where is the celebrity threshold?Where the fan-out time for one post exceeds the freshness target; tune from fan-out lag.
How do you shard the timeline cache?By user id; every operation touches one user's key.
New posts while the user is scrolling?Keep the cursor stable and show a "new posts" marker that reloads from the top.

Senior signal: you compute the fan-out multiplier before choosing a strategy, treat the timeline as a rebuildable cache and not a source of truth, and skip inactive users without being asked.

Chat and messaging

Part 8 of 9 · stateful connections, ordered delivery

Deliver messages between users in real time, in order, without loss, whether or not the recipient is online. It is asked because it is the standard stateful system: long-lived connections, routing to the right server, ordering and offline sync.

  • Requirements and scale
  • API and data model
  • High-level design
  • Deep dives: connection layer, 1:1 and group flows, receipts and ordering, offline delivery, presence, multi-device, encryption
  • Trade-offs and follow-ups

Requirements and scale

Chat and messaging

  • Functional: 1:1 and group chat (up to about 1,000 members); sent, delivered and read receipts; presence and last seen; delivery to offline users with a push notification; history synced across a user's devices.
  • Non-functional: under 500 ms end to end at p99 when both sides are online; no acknowledged message is lost; messages in one conversation appear in the same order for everyone; 100 M concurrent connections.
  • Out of scope: voice and video calls, the media pipeline (same as the feed: object store plus CDN), spam detection.
QuantityArithmeticResult (approx.)
UsersAssumption500 M DAU
Messages500 M x 40 per day = 20 B / 86,400 s230,000 per second average, 700,000 peak (3x)
Connections20% of DAU online at peak100 M concurrent
Gateway servers100 M / 100,000 connections per server1,000 servers
Storage20 B x 200 bytes per day x 3654 TB per day, 1.5 PB per year before replication
Bandwidth230,000 x 200 bytes46 MB per second average, 140 MB per second peak (text only)

What the numbers say: write-heavy, with reads mostly of recent messages. Connection count, not QPS, sizes the gateway tier; message volume sizes the store.

API and data model

Chat and messaging

  • Store: a wide-column store (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase): append-heavy writes, range reads within a partition, linear scale-out. Bucket very large conversations by month so no partition grows without bound.
  • Also needed: the same MEMBER data keyed by user (the inbox), so "my conversations, most recent first" is one query.

High-level design

Chat and messaging

  • Connect: the client opens a WebSocket to a gateway through a load balancer; the gateway authenticates it and writes user, device and gateway into the session registry.
  • Send: gateway forwards to the chat service, which assigns the next seq for the conversation, persists the message, and acks the sender.
  • Deliver: for each recipient device the chat service finds the gateway in the registry and pushes the message down that connection.
  • Offline: no session means a push notification; the message waits in the store until the device reconnects and pulls everything after its last seq.
  • Presence: gateways report heartbeats to a separate service, so presence load cannot slow messaging.

Deep dives

Chat and messaging

Connection layer and session registry

TransportGainCost
WebSocketFull duplex, low overhead per messageStateful servers, sticky connections, careful deploys
Long pollingWorks through any proxyA request per message, higher latency; keep as fallback
Server-sent eventsSimple server pushOne direction only; sends need separate requests
  • Registry: Redis, session:{user_id} to a map of device id to gateway id, with a TTL refreshed by heartbeats (about every 30 s).
  • Routing: the chat service calls the gateway directly (RPC) or publishes to a per-gateway channel; never broadcast to all gateways.
  • Gateway dies: its connections drop, clients reconnect with backoff and jitter to another gateway, registry entries are overwritten or expire. In-flight messages are safe because they were persisted before delivery.
  • Deploys: drain gateways gradually; 100,000 clients reconnecting at once is a self-made thundering herd.

1:1 message flow, receipts and ordering

  • Ordering: the server assigns a per-conversation, strictly increasing seq. Client timestamps are untrusted and are used only for display.
  • Assigning seq: route all writes for a conversation to one owner (partition by conversation id) and increment there, or use an atomic counter or conditional write per conversation. A global sequence is unnecessary and would be a bottleneck.
  • No loss, no duplicates: the client retries a send with the same client_msg_id until acked; the server deduplicates on it. A device that sees seq 44 after 42 knows it must fetch 43.

Group message flow

  • Small groups: fan out on send as shown.
  • Very large groups or channels: stop pushing every message; send a lightweight "new activity" signal and let clients pull by after_seq. Read receipts become counts or are switched off.
  • Batch the registry lookups and group deliveries per gateway, so a 1,000 member group costs tens of calls, not a thousand.

Offline delivery, multi-device sync and presence

TopicDesignWatch for
Offline deliveryMessage stays in the store; a push notification wakes the app; on reconnect the device pulls each changed conversation after its last seqPush is best effort and may be dropped; correctness comes from the pull
Multi-deviceEach device is its own session and keeps its own sync position; the sender's other devices receive the message tooRead state is per user, delivery state per device
PresenceHeartbeat sets a key with a short TTL; no heartbeat means offline; last seen is written on disconnectFlapping on bad networks: delay the offline transition by a few seconds
Presence fan-outPush changes only to users currently viewing that contact or chat; otherwise fetch on openPushing every change to every contact is quadratic

End-to-end encryption

With end-to-end encryption (the Signal protocol is the widely documented design), clients publish public keys through the server and encrypt each message for every recipient device, so the server stores and routes only ciphertext it cannot read. The architecture above is unchanged, but server-side search and content moderation are no longer possible, and adding a device, restoring history and group membership changes all become key management problems.

Trade-offs and follow-ups

Chat and messaging

DecisionChoiceAlternativeWhy
TransportWebSocketLong pollingLatency and overhead at 100 M connections
OrderingPer-conversation seq from the serverClient or wall-clock timestampsTotal order per conversation, gap detection
StorageWide-column, partition by conversationRelationalWrite volume and range reads
Delivery guaranteeAt-least-once plus client dedupAt-most-onceLost messages are unacceptable
Group storageOne copy per conversationOne copy per recipient inboxStorage and write cost; the per-recipient copy is simpler only for tiny groups
  • Failure mode: stale registry entry points to a dead gateway. Delivery fails fast, the entry is removed, and the offline path (push plus pull) takes over.
  • Failure mode: reconnect storm after a network blip. Jittered backoff on clients, admission control on gateways.
  • Failure mode: hot conversation partition (a huge active group). Time-bucket the partition and switch the group to pull.
Follow-upOne-line answer
Typing indicators?Ephemeral events through the same connection, never persisted, dropped under load.
Message search?A separate index fed asynchronously; on the device only if end-to-end encrypted.
Multi-region?Users connect to the nearest region; a conversation has a home region for seq assignment, or accept per-region order with a merge rule.
Why not Kafka as the message store?It suits transport between services, not per-conversation random reads over years of history.

Senior signal: you state the invariant "persist, then ack, then deliver", make the pull by seq the source of correctness with push as an optimisation, and separate the stateful gateway tier from the stateless logic.

Search autocomplete

Part 9 of 9 · precomputed answers, tight latency

Return the top few completions for each prefix a user types. It is asked because the read path must be nearly free, which pushes all the work into an offline index build and layers of caching.

  • Requirements and scale
  • API and data model
  • High-level design
  • Deep dives: trie versus precomputed top-k, building the index, serving and caching, sharding, ranking, filtering
  • Trade-offs and follow-ups

Requirements and scale

Search autocomplete

  • Functional: up to 8 suggestions for a prefix; ranked by popularity; trending queries appear within minutes; unsafe or blocked suggestions never shown.
  • Non-functional: under 100 ms end to end at p99, under 10 ms inside the service; highly available (degrade to no suggestions, never block search); results may be minutes stale.
  • Out of scope: the search results themselves, spelling correction, deep personalisation.
QuantityArithmeticResult (approx.)
UsersAssumption100 M DAU
Searches100 M x 10 per day1 B per day
Suggest requests1 B x 6 per search (after debounce) = 6 B / 86,400 s70,000 per second average, 210,000 peak (3x)
Index size50 M prefixes x (20 byte key + 10 x 30 bytes)16 GB, fits in RAM on one machine
Query log1 B x 100 bytes100 GB per day
Bandwidth70,000 x 500 bytes35 MB per second average, 105 MB per second peak

What the numbers say: the index is small and the request rate is large. You replicate for throughput long before you need to shard for size, and every request you answer from a cache is one the service never sees.

API and data model

Search autocomplete

DataShapeStore and reason
Prefix indexNormalised prefix (up to 20 characters) to an ordered list of up to 10 (query, score)Immutable, versioned files built offline and loaded into memory by the suggest service; a published snapshot is never edited
Query countsQuery, language, time bucket, countBatch tables in the data lake; input to the build
Trending deltaQuery to recent count, last few hoursSmall in-memory or Redis structure fed by a stream job
BlocklistTerms and patternsSmall table, pushed to builders and servers

High-level design

Search autocomplete

  • Read: the browser asks the CDN; on a miss the suggest service normalises the prefix, looks it up in memory, merges any trending entries, filters, and returns with a cache lifetime.
  • Log: completed searches (not keystrokes) go to the query log asynchronously.
  • Batch build: every hour or day, aggregate counts with time decay, drop rare and blocked queries, compute the top k for every prefix, publish a snapshot.
  • Swap: servers load the new snapshot beside the old one and switch atomically; a bad build is rolled back by pointing at the previous version.
  • Streaming: a stream job counts queries over a sliding window and feeds a small trending delta, so breaking topics do not wait for the next batch.

Deep dives

Search autocomplete

Trie versus precomputed top-k per prefix

StructureLookupMemoryUpdatesUse when
Plain trie, counts at leavesWalk the prefix, then search the subtree: slow for short prefixesSmallestCheapNever for serving
Trie with top-k at each nodeO(prefix length)Medium; prefixes share structureA count change touches every ancestorIn-process index on one machine
Hash map: prefix to top-kO(1)Largest; each prefix stored in fullRebuild offlineSimple sharding and KV or CDN friendly; the usual choice

Both serving structures are the same idea: the answer for every prefix is computed before anyone asks. Limit prefix length (about 20) and keep only prefixes of queries above a count threshold.

Building the index: batch plus streaming

Batch buildStreaming update
InputDays or weeks of query logsThe live event stream, sliding window of minutes to hours
OutputA complete, versioned snapshotA small delta of trending queries
FreshnessHoursMinutes
StrengthSimple, reproducible, easy to roll backCatches breaking topics
WeaknessStale between buildsApproximate counts, easier to game; needs stricter filtering
  • Score with a decayed count (recent days weigh more) so last year's event does not outrank today's.
  • Sampling the log (1 in 10) is fine for popular queries and cuts build cost.

Serving path, caching and the latency budget

LayerWhat it doesBudget (approx.)
BrowserDebounce, cancel superseded requests, cache results per prefix for the session0 ms on a hit
Network to the edgeOne round trip on a kept-alive connection20 to 50 ms
CDNCaches by full URL for minutes1 to 5 ms
Edge to origin (miss only)Round trip to the nearest region10 to 30 ms
Suggest serviceNormalise, look up, merge, filter1 to 5 ms

Sharding the index

  • First question: does it need sharding at all? At 16 GB, no: run many identical replicas per region. Shard when languages, markets or longer prefixes push it past one machine's memory.
  • Hash of the prefix: even load, and works because a lookup is an exact key match. The natural choice for the prefix map.
  • Range by leading characters: needed for a real trie; ranges must be sized from the measured distribution (s is far busier than x) and kept in a shard map.

Ranking, personalisation and filtering

  • Ranking: decayed frequency, optionally adjusted by click-through on the suggestion and by language or region (a separate index per market keeps responses cacheable).
  • Personalisation: per-user responses cannot be shared in a CDN. Keep the global list cacheable and blend the user's own recent searches on the client.
  • Filtering at build time: blocklist, classifiers for offensive or dangerous content, and a minimum number of distinct users per query so one person's private query can never be suggested.
  • Filtering at serve time: a small blocklist checked on every response, so a takedown works in minutes without a rebuild; purge the CDN for the affected prefixes.

Trade-offs and follow-ups

Search autocomplete

DecisionChoiceAlternativeWhy
IndexPrecomputed top-k per prefixSearch a trie at query timeConstant-time reads, cacheable
UpdatesImmutable snapshots plus a trending deltaUpdate the index in place per querySimple servers, safe rollback
Scale-outReplicas first, shards laterShard from the startThe index is small; QPS is the constraint
PersonalisationOn the clientOn the serverKeeps CDN caching
  • Failure mode: a bad index build ships empty or offensive results. Validate the snapshot (size, sample queries), roll out to a few servers first, keep the previous version loaded.
  • Failure mode: manipulation. Coordinated queries push a phrase into suggestions; count distinct users, cap per-user contribution, review fast risers.
  • Failure mode: suggest service down. The search box still works; the client hides the dropdown after a short timeout.
Follow-upOne-line answer
Typos and fuzzy matching?Out of the basic design; add an edit-distance pass or a separate spelling service for prefixes with no results.
Matching in the middle of a phrase?Index word-level prefixes as extra keys; costs index size.
Many languages?An index per language with language-specific normalisation; the request carries the language.
How fresh is fresh enough?Hourly batch covers almost all traffic; the trending delta covers news events.

Senior signal: you notice from the estimate that the index fits in memory and say "replicate, do not shard", put most of the latency budget on the network and caches, and treat filtering as a first-class requirement.

Cheat sheet

One line per case. If you can rebuild the design from its row, you know it.

CaseCore ideaKey data storeHardest deep dive
URL shortenerA cached point lookup; keys from counter ranges, redirect with 302Hash-sharded KV store plus RedisKey generation without collisions or coordination per write
Rate limiterAtomic check-and-count per key at the gatewayRedis with Lua scriptsAccuracy versus a hop per request; behaviour when Redis is down
Key-value storeConsistent hashing plus leaderless N / W / R quorums, repaired in the backgroundLSM tree on each nodeConflict resolution and the four repair mechanisms
Unique ID generatorTimestamp, worker id and sequence packed into 64 bits, generated locallyNone (etcd only for worker leases)Clock going backwards and duplicate worker ids
Notification systemQueue per channel and priority, at-least-once with deduplicationMessage queues plus a wide-column delivery logRetries that neither duplicate nor storm; provider failover
News feedPrecompute timelines by fan-out on write, pull for celebritiesRedis sorted sets of post idsHybrid fan-out and its threshold
ChatPersist, ack, deliver through the gateway that holds the connection; sync by per-conversation seqWide-column store partitioned by conversationOrdering and gap-free delivery across devices and reconnects
Search autocompletePrecompute top-k for every prefix offline, serve from memory and cachesImmutable in-memory prefix indexFreshness of the index without giving up cacheability
  • Patterns that repeat: keep the hot path to one lookup; move work to write time or offline when reads dominate; put a queue wherever a slow or external dependency sits; treat caches and derived views as rebuildable.
  • Questions that repeat: what is the hot key, what happens when the cache or queue is down, where can a duplicate appear, what changes at 10x.
